h. Consumable Natural Resources
During the initial stages of project execution moderate amounts of natural resources will be consumed by project construction activities. Bituminous material and stone for street construction; lumber, copper and steel and concrete for buildings; and energy to power the construction equipment are but a few of the items.
When an existing building within the project is demolished, natural resources will be required to replace it as part of the housing stock, directly or indirectly. The demolition of 119 structures in the project will have a negative impact in this regard.
Although the rehabilitation of project properties will consume amounts of natural resources, the rehabilitation process will obviate the need to further destroy additional natural resources (already in place from previous years) in the form of existing housing. The extensive use of rehabilitation for the area is major positive factor in this regard. Code enforcement activities are likewise considered as to have a positive impact, but to a lesser degree.
Power needed for the additional project lighting, estimated previously at 70 KW per day, or approximately the power requirement of two residential homes, will be in addition to the areas present power needs. Based on PP&L's power generation sources, this energy will most likely come from coal mined in Pennsylvania. The amount of coal consumed in providing this much energy is a exceptionally small when compared to the increased advantages provided by lighting of the area.
i. Parking
The areas available for parking within the project will be expanded and will have a positive impact on residential land use and the commercial areas in the project. These parking sites are evenly distributed throughout the project and will, in many cases, be an adjunct to the system of open spaces planned. Like open spaces, they will serve to reduce the population density of the area.
The parking areas will be paved. Additional amounts of paved surface will increase the run-off and lower the water table to some minor degree. Since the urban area does not depend on groundwater for its water supply, this is disregarded as a negative factor.
